http://www.thejewishstar.com/stories/98-.text: Wednesday, September 23, 2026 Complete forecast 98-year-old survivor: Hatred won’t define you As Jewish students around the world begin a new academic year amid heightened antisemitism, a 98-year-old Holocaust survivor is urging them to stand proudly as Jews and never allow hatred to define them. The International March of the Living launched a global initiative on Sept. 1 — the 87th anniversary of the outbreak of World War II — centered on an open letter from survivor and educator Nate Leipciger to Jewish students returning to school. “Antisemitism is old. Your future is not,” he writes. In 1948, Nate immigrated to Canada, where he married Bernice. They had three daughters, and he later became a grandfather of 16 and great-grandfather of 12. Here is his letter: Dear Jewish students, My name is Nate Leipciger, and I am a 98-year-old Holocaust survivor. Today marks the 87th anniversary of the outbreak of World War II — the day that changed my life, and the lives of so many others, forever. I was 15 years old when the Nazis deported my family from the ghetto to Auschwitz-Birkenau. My father and I survived together. Most of our family did not. As a new academic year begins, I am writing because many of you are returning to campus carrying more than books, plans and ambitions. Since Oct. 7, 2023, you have also carried grief, fear, anger and a painful awareness of how quickly antisemitism can enter spaces that promise knowledge, openness and belonging. You may have seen the murder and kidnapping of Jews met with excuses, celebration or silence. You may have heard ancient accusations in modern language, or been asked to answer for distant events before anyone asked whether you were mourning, afraid or safe. Some of you have wondered whether to hide a Star of David, a kippah or your voice. Please remember: You are not responsible for the hatred directed at you. You do not have to conceal who you are to earn the right to belong. Never permit those who hate you to define you. … A university should be a place where evidence matters, difficult questions are examined honestly and disagreement never becomes intimidation. Criticism of any government, including Israel’s, is legitimate. Harassing or excluding Jewish students, celebrating violence against Jews or demanding that they renounce part of their identity is not criticism. It is discrimination. Do not allow anyone to force you into a false choice between your Jewish identity and your place in the wider world. Jewish identity is not merely a response to persecution. It is an inheritance of faith, learning, family, creativity, justice and hope. Across millennia, Jews have studied, questioned, prayed and thrived. We are defined by what we create and carry forward. Learn that inheritance. Read Jewish history beyond persecution. Ask your family for its stories. Enter a synagogue, a Jewish student center or a Shabbat table. Learn a Hebrew word, a melody or a page of text. The more deeply you know who you are, the less power a slogan has to define you. No one should demand that you deny Jewish history, disown the Jewish people or surrender your connection to Israel. For those of us who lived when Jews had nowhere safe to turn, a Jewish homeland is not an abstraction. It is an answer to Jewish powerlessness. … Be courageous, but do not stand alone. Find one another. Support the classmate who is afraid or isolated. Build alliances. Stand against racism, hatred of other minorities and every form of dehumanization and discrimination. Just as importantly, diligently study Jewish history so that you are able to confront the lies and propaganda being spread against the Jewish people and the Jewish state. Jewish pride is strongest when joined with moral courage. I would like to remind you that during the Holocaust, Jewish youth made the ultimate sacrifice to preserve the dignity and honor of the Jewish people — fighting to their deaths in the Warsaw Ghetto and across Nazi-occupied Europe. Today, we do not ask you to risk your lives. But please be aware that there are others, the same age as you, who put their young lives at risk every day in the State of Israel, defending the Jewish state and the future of the Jewish people. After everything I witnessed, people ask how I can still have hope. I have hope because I have seen Jewish life rebuilt. … The future of Jewish life is passing into your hands. Carry it without apology, with compassion and strength. You belong to a people that has endured exile, persecution and attempts at erasure, yet continues to learn, celebrate, love and hope. Antisemitism is old. Your future is not. This initiative is being promoted in partnership with Jewish and Zionist student organizations worldwide including the World Union of Jewish Students, the Jewish Agency for Israel, ASHER, the World Zionist Organization, the Israeli-American Council and Students Supporting Israel. Photograph: Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Starlink access restored, says UK’s Streeting after Hegseth meeting UK defence secretary says Pete Hegseth assured him satellite communications system back up and running in Ukraine. What we know on day 1,696 Guardian staff and agencies Thu 15 Oct 2026 20.43 EDT Last modified on Thu 15 Oct 2026 21.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukraine’s access to Elon Musk’s Starlink had been restored, according to UK defence secretary Wes Streeting. Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted on Wednesday, hampering the country’s attack and air-defence drone missions, and triggering a new rift between Washington and Kyiv. On Thursday, Streeting said his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system was back up and running. He said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.” The order to limit Starlink access came from inside the White House , according to a report by Reuters, citing two US officials and a western official briefed on the matter. The ⁠officials said leaders at the defence ⁠department received a message that the service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed. The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which ⁠is the military-grade version of the Starlink service . Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, Ukrainoan president Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Nato chief Mark Rutte in Brussels and held a string of bilateral meetings with European leaders before he was set to join an EU summit on Friday. French president Emmanuel Macron on Thursday said it was “crucial” that Ukraine receive “all the means necessary to protect itself” after meeting Zelenskyy. “I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE,” Polish prime minister Donald Tusk posted online. Vladimir Putin has said that recent ⁠Ukrainian ​strikes on Russian oil refineries had not caused significant ⁠damage and vowed that Moscow would respond. “They ⁠hit here and there. Nothing ​particularly significant. Nevertheless ‌they are ‌carrying on,” the Russian president was quoted as saying by the Interfax news agency. His comments ‌came after a major Ukrainian drone attack ignited a fire at an oil refinery in Russia’s Ryazan region on Thursday morning, according ‌to the regional governor. It was the first confirmed ​Ukrainian attack on a Russian energy facility since US president Donald Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to. The US treasury department has extended a sanctions waiver on Russian oil company Lukoil for service stations outside Russia through April 2027. Thursday’s announcement allows Lukoil-branded stations in countries like the US to continue serving customers until 24 April next year. The extension comes a week after Trump said he had secured an agreement with Russia to supply diesel to American and global markets, with the US treasury issuing a temporary licence to enable flows. The latest licence, like an earlier one, does not allow the “transfer of funds to any person or account located in the Russian Federation”. Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours , Ukraine’s emergency services said Thursday. Between midnight and Thursday morning, Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, Zelenskyy said on X. He added that the barrage came “precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted,” an apparent reference to the Starlink restrictions on drones. Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said. https://www.irishdentist.ie/queen-budape.text: Politics October 4, 2026 Queen Budapest ’86 at the cinema: when rock crossed the Iron Curtain Restored in 4K from the original 35mm footage, Queen’s concert at the Népstadion returns to cinemas from 7 October On 27 July 1986, at the Népstadion in Budapest, eighty thousand people gathered to attend a concert destined to push the boundaries of music . Queen were in the midst of Magic Tour : Freddie Mercury, Brian May, Roger Taylor and John Deacon brought a show of strength and precision to the stage, just five concerts before the band’s last performance with Mercury. That evening was also Queen’s last live performance with Freddie to be filmed. What made the event exceptional was the location, as well as its scale. In a Europe divided by the Iron Curtain, i Queen were the first Western rock band to perform in Hungary . The stadium audience was joined by an estimated 45,000 people who remained outside, close enough to hear the music. Some fans arrived from Russia and Poland: a journey to a concert which, for many, also meant getting closer to a world that had until then been distant. The scale of the undertaking is reflected in its documentation. The concert was filmed in 35 mm by the best Hungarian cinematographers, with 17 cameras and approximately 40 kilometers of film. The operation was approved by the Hungarian government: an unprecedented event for a communist state. The result was a rare visual testimony, which conveys both the energy of the show and the historical weight of that evening. Now Queen Budapest returns to the big screen in a new version restored in 4K, created from the original footage at Park Road Post Production, Peter Jackson’s New Zealand studio. The sound has also been renewed thanks to the original multitrack recordings. In the film, directed by János Zsombolyai and distributed by Sony Music Vision, Brian May and Roger Taylor look back on the concert and its lasting cultural impact. The two musicians also attended the London premiere. The setlist runs through some of Queen’s most beloved songs, from “We Will Rock You” and “We Are the Champions” to “Under Pressure” and “Bohemian Rhapsody.” Among the most singular moments, the acoustic arrangement of “Tavaszi Szél Vizet Áraszt”, a Hungarian folk song which, that evening, brought the band closer to the culture of the country that hosted them. From October 7th Queen Budapest will be in cinemas and IMAX theaters around the world, with distribution by Trafalgar Releasing. In Italy the film will be exclusive from 7 to 11 October . Tickets are available on nexostudios.it. The soundtrack will also be released on November 6, remixed by the Queen studio team from the original multitrack recordings. Released internationally by Legacy Recordings and in the United States and Canada by Hollywood Records, it will be available digitally, as a double CD and, for the first time, in a 3LP box set. The Blu-ray and DVD editions will also arrive on the same date.
